overview.headline: How wing size and reference area determine lift and why flaps extend for landing

keyPoints.point: Lift is directly proportional to area so doubling area doubles lift
keyPoints.quote: Like the other aerodynamic force, drag, the lift is directly proportional to the area of the object.

keyPoints.point: Total aerodynamic force equals pressure times surface area around body
keyPoints.quote: The total aerodynamic force is equal to the pressure times the surface area around the body.

keyPoints.point: Wing planform area viewed from above is logical reference area for lift
keyPoints.quote: the logical choice is the wing planform area.

keyPoints.point: Designers increase wing area with flaps and slats during takeoff and landing
keyPoints.quote: This is done by sliding the flaps backwards along metal tracks and shifting the slats forward to increase the wing area.

keyTerms.gloss: aerodynamic force perpendicular to flight direction that varies with pressure
keyTerms.quote: Lift is the component of this force perpendicular to the flight direction.

keyTerms.gloss: other aerodynamic force that also varies directly with area
keyTerms.quote: Like the other aerodynamic force, drag, the lift is directly proportional to the area of the object.

keyTerms.gloss: area of wing seen from above used as reference area for lift calculations
keyTerms.quote: The planform area is the area of the wing as viewed from above the wing, looking along the “lift” direction.

keyTerms.gloss: value experimentally determined by measuring lift and area that adjusts with reference area
keyTerms.quote: the lift coefficient is determined experimentally

keyTerms.gloss: movable wing parts slid backwards to increase area for low velocity takeoff and landing
keyTerms.quote: This is done by sliding the flaps backwards along metal tracks and shifting the slats forward to increase the wing area.
